I study my yard at all different times of the day to see where the sun shines and for what length of time and what native plants do best. Research how to enrich the soil without using toxic chemicals. I’ve been dreaming of this my entire life. a_revoir.message:
Elleira Drassel What “value judgement”?

Again. I urge you to learn something about milkweed and about the collection of the fluff and seeds.

Milkweed is an annual not a perennial. The plant dies at the end of the season. The wind distributes the fluff which have the seed attached. They can drift miles.

By the time the milkweed fluff is harvested, the plant is dead. It is of no value to anyone.

The seeds are knocked off the fluff and distributed in the fields the plants came from to ensure another crop the next year.

The harvesting the seeds ensures that they can be distributed not just from the field they cane from but to home gardens, butterfly gardens…

This is already in practice and has been for years.

What is more dangerous to butterflies is NOT distributing the seeds. And USING the fluff ensures that there are MORE plants to attract Monarchs, not less.

If the demand for the use of the fluff increases it means that MORE fields will be needed and that means that there are more habitats for butterflies.

As for your nonsense about “unscrupulous suppliers preventing plants from reseeding” they don’t need the seeds, they aren’t going out to fields to “harvest” them. It’s time-consuming and there is no “monetization” possible. There’s no “Big Fluff” conspiracy.

Your arguments just not based on facts.

a_revoir.message: The problem with some seed bombs (don't know the specific of these) is that they contain either too many seeds of one species or many species.  Many seed species may not even be native to that area.  Not all plants have the same growing condition needs.  Not all seed species, in a ball,  will germinate and grow where they are placed.  If there are too many seeds in a ball then competition occurs and they can't thrive.  Seed packets all recommend seed spacing.  This isn't taken into account with a seed ball.  I made my own seed balls with only 3-4 seeds of one species in each.  I still had limited success.

a_revoir.message:
Eric Selin In my rural neighborhood there is also no shortage of neighbors spraying pesticides and/or herbicides on beans and corn with no attention to drift. Don't assume your seeds are to blame. 

A member of the farm bureau came out to view the damage our neighbor's  spraying had caused. He told us we couldn't blame the corn and bean farmer we witnessed spraying adjacent to our now damaged flowers and trees. This despite the direct 10+ mph wind our on site windsock showed at the time. The farm bureau rep explained that even on seemingly still, hot days the spray can drift in the air for a mile or more before it sinks fully down to do it's damage. So we couldn't be sure which local corn or bean farmer was to blame. 

    Since then only a corner of our property sheltered by between two buildings still supports a few dozen or so native milkweed plants every year.

a_revoir.message:
My mother was born in 1933.  She remembered collecting milkweed pods and selling them to "the government" as a child.

A few years back I looked up why?

The answer:

Latex is the sap of the rubber tree plant.  It is used to make natural rubber.  During WW II, demand was high and getting it (from the tropics) was difficult, so the federal government grew milkweed and used the milkweed sap as a substitute.

a_revoir.message: Cindy MoodyYou’ve got to be careful about what Milkweed you buy. The non native varieties are a caterpillar’s favorite, but those big caterpillars grow into butterflies that are often much weaker and don’t make it through migration. It’s like growing a child on candy, they eat a lot sure, but they don’t get the nutrition required to grow up healthy. A lot of people buy the tropical Milkweed because they like the brighter flowers and narrow leaves, but it’s actually harmful to the Monarchs in the long-run.

To my understanding, wasps are territorial and if they believe another nest to be there, they’ll go away. My butterfly garden is currently..under construction haha, but when it was thriving, I ordered a 2 pack, hung them up in sort of adjacent corners from the garden and the wasps seemed to bugger off. The lizards on the other hand are a different story. They do make lizard products to mitigate them like sprays and traps but I don’t know if the sprays and such are toxic for the butterflies/bees. If you have a porch, could try keeping some plants there as feeders when you find caterpillars outside and then they’ll chrysalis on the screen. a_revoir.message: Marie Frisa I live in Tucson, Arizona and I have a bunch of milkweed that the monarchs lay their eggs on. Mine are under a Palo Verde tree however, the morning sun does hit them as well as late evening sun but they dont get full evening sun.  There is a big yellow bells bush next to it. That filter is the evening sun.  They don’t need a lot of water once established nor do they like it.  Mine are on a drip system that waters daily however, the tip is a sprayer that’s raised up high, so it basically gives them a shower and doesn’t saturate the soil.   It’s just enough water, but not too much.  They can do really well here in Arizona as long as they are not in full sun all day long.  Never get just one bush.  Monarchs will lay their eggs and one bush is not even enough food for one single caterpillar never mind hundreds.  They will run out of food and die.  I was told to buy a minimum of seven plants with several ranches on each and I think that is the bare minimum.  If you were closer to me, I would give you seeds because I have so many of them that just get tossed back into the soil.  I could actually mail you seeds as well.  ￼￼￼Each plant produces tons of seeds that then fall to the ground or I throw them on the ground and the following year I get tons of new plants popping up. ￼ by the middle of summer there is hardly a leaf left from all the monarchs that lay their eggs and I have a little forest going.  I have given many plants away once they are mature enough to put into pots.  At the nurseries that I bought mine from it was $19.99 for a single stem milkweed with no branches and roughly about 15 inches tall.  You are supposed to cut them back in the winter and when they grow again, they will grow multiple branches.  The plants they sell with multiple branches go for $39.99.  They are ridiculously expensive and yet super easy to grow and get seeds from so I don’t get it.   This is why I give seeds away and even plants.  I want more people to grow these for our beautiful monarchs.  ￼￼￼

a_revoir.message:
NOT on VANCOUVER ISLAND !!!!!                                                                             How campaigns to save the monarch butterfly can threaten Vancouver Island’s biodiversity
Campaigns mailing out milkweed seeds for monarch butterflies could be introducing more invasive species to Vancouver Island, experts say.
BY LYS MORTON ● NANAIMO, VANCOUVER ISLAND ● MAY 4, 2023

Monarch butterfly on some flowers, orange wings spread open
While you can find monarch butterflies on Vancouver Island at places like Coombs Butterfly World, they are not native to the region. Photo by Lys Morton
Monarch butterflies were officially declared endangered in 2022, the latest species to struggle with the effects of the climate crisis and agricultural activities. 

You may have noticed a call to action to plant milkweed, the main food source and nesting point for monarch butterflies. 

But ads to mail in a self-addressed envelope for milkweed seeds harkens back to previous ill-fated “protect the pollinators” campaigns. 

General Mills’ Bring Back the Bees program has come under scrutiny for sending packages of wildflower seeds to areas where the plants are invasive, costing regional conservation groups time and resources keeping their local ecosystems safe. 

Monarch butterflies summer through most of the northeast United States and southeast Canada then travel upwards of 4,500 kilometers south to winter in Mexico. They don’t typically travel through Vancouver Island. 

Though sightings have been recorded here and there, the BC Conservation Data Centre believes these events are most likely the result of enthusiasts hatching eggs in backyards or monarch butterflies from the mainland being blown west. 

As monarchs continue to be threatened by habitat loss and as warming temperatures change their migratory patterns to include more of the Pacific Northwest, scientists have observed a stronger presence of the butterfly throughout southern B.C.

It turns out, B.C.’s showy milkweed (Asclepias speciosa) isn’t native to Vancouver Island either. The perennial is found naturally throughout the province’s southern Interior but transplanted as a garden plant on Vancouver Island. The large reddish purple flowers blossom to show delicate white stars in a show that competes with the sizable blooms of rhododendrons.

“Sixty per cent of invasive species are planted by humans, often purchasing from stores and nurseries,” Gail Wallin, executive director of Invasive Species Council of BC explains to The Discourse. “Some milkweed species are going to be very invasive to Vancouver Island and should be avoided. Others you could plant and properly manage and it will be more classified as an exotic species.”

It’s easy to picture good samaritans around the Island planting an abundance of showy milkweed, only to have the plant become the next Scotch broom. But Wallin advises locals to research what plants are native to your area and focus energy there.

“Be PlantWise,” Wallin says, referring to the Invasive Species Council of BC’s education program that helps gardeners identify invasive species and replace them with native substitutes. ISCBC also reaches out to nurseries around BC and helps them halt the sales of invasive species. “Know what’s in your garden, what’s in your area. If invasive species are being sold to you, contact us and we have means to deal with that.”

Environmental Educator Hunter Jarratt tells The Discourse mail-in seed packets are the latest in well-meaning actions doing damage.

“A lot of people are wanting to do their part to help fix the climate crisis, the biodiversity crisis. We want to feel good, like we’re doing something. At the same time there are companies that are kind of preying on that.”

With 60 different native species of butterflies on Vancouver Island, creating a pollinator habitat garden is sure to bring some of them to your green space. Hunter says focusing on learning what your region supports and helping identify invasive species can create larger impacts than focusing on just one species. 

Local organizations like Nanaimo and Area Land Trust offer native plant starters such as pearly everlasting and trailing blackberry, the native counter to the invasive Himalayan blackberry. 

Programs to report invasive species in your area can help identify what range invasive species have overtaken and where to focus conservation and land management resources.

“That information gets sent right to professionals,” Hunter explains. “And they can get back to you and provide you with more information. And also, we can then include that in management plans.”

In the Nanaimo region, residents are encouraged to use the Report-A-Weed app and start up a volunteer work party to remove invasive species. 

While recent reports from the Mexico branch of the World Wildlife Federation say monarch butterfly populations are still falling, recovery strategies for B.C.’s own at-risk species continue to be updated with actions residents can take. 

A 2021 assessment of the Edward’s Beach Moth advised continued conservation efforts throughout the Gulf Islands and smaller islands in the Salish Sea.

a_revoir.message: Frances Cheetham the best way to plant milkweed is to get seeds from a local pod(s) obtained for free by going on a nature walk in a natural area near where you live. And I am assuming, but not sure, that you both a) get a frost in winter and b) are willing to plant common milkweed. If this is true: plant milkweed seeds in the top 1/2 inch of average garden soil, lightly covered, in October. You get Milkweed in the spring. Milkweed needs weeks of cold damp temperarures to germinate. Lots of people start Milkweed indoors but its a project. You can also but Swamp Milkweed at reputable independent nursuries. It is not reccomended to buy from big box stores. Milkweed likes full sun medium sun and some sun never full shade. It likes to grow in clumps. It loves to grow on the edges of fields. I have given about 1/3 of my garden borders and veg gardens up to creating a Milkweed ecosystem and its actually nice and now I just go to the farmers market for the most part instead of producing not so great veggies. I still grow tomatos basil herbs and cukes but I gave the squash  and onion area up to Milkweed and have not looked back. Surely you can buy the seeds here as well just make sure you get the exact local native ones for your exact area .

a_revoir.message: Please just don't forget. Native milkweed seeds require a 30-60 day period of cold stratification to germinate. You can find videos on-line about how to do this. Also, when growing ANY perennial plant from seed, it's highly advised you cut any flower buds off the 1st 1-2 years to give the plant a chance to establish thoroughly. Some perennials - if allowed to flower heavily in their 1st year - may act like an annual and peter out after year 1. Flowering takes huge amounts of resources, and if the plant's thinking, "well, I've reproduced," it will not give it's roots enough resources and then they're done.

a_revoir.message: Penny Horning I bought my house in 2011 and, within two years, I extricated several useless hedges.  I planted a few sedum plants and the milkweed happily planted themselves.  After a few years I had a forest in my front yard, I counted well over 100 plants.  But, I had health problems and let my neighbor help me with mowing the front yard.  The milkweed forest was along the borders of the lawn, which he has pushed back to get rid of the milkweed.  His yard is one large, empty lawn.  This past autumn, I allowed him to clean out the overgrown jungle that was my backyard.  I saved what was left of the remaining milkweed pods to plant the seeds in the backyard this spring, now that I'm retired and will have more time.  I've only ever seen one Monarch caterpillar, but I refuse to give up!

a_revoir.message: If you buy native, specifically for your zone, it should be okay. There are around 115 species of milkweed. The only one I know that could be invasive is common milkweed, Asclepias Syriaca. It spreads aggressively through rhizomes. a_revoir.message: Lisa Allen Colvin The term “invasive” is not used for native plants; the word “aggressive” is the proper term. Common milkweed (Asclepias syriaca) is an aggressive spreader via its underground roots; others are much less aggressive, spreading mainly by seed. According to Monarch Watch, there are 73 species of native milkweeds in the United States. Many of which are rare, threatened, and endangered. Monarchs utilize about 30 of these species as host plants with some regularity. Check with your local Extension office to find out which are native to your area and plant those, while avoiding common milkweed if you wish to support mnarchs yet still have a neat garden!
a_revoir.motif: long commentaire expert entre abonnes, exact dans lensemble ; la distinction agressif contre envahissant a deja ete publiee

a_revoir.message:
Native plants aren't weeds. Colonizers came over and decided green short grass lawns and plants from overseas are great, and native plants, shrubs, trees, sedges, and grasses are weeds.

Native plants bring more nutrients and water into the soil with longer root systems. They host native beneficial insects, that in turn feed birds and other animals, and pollinate more plants than the European honeybee. Many pollinators are specialized and are made for specific native plants. Native plants are beautiful, and one established, don't require watering and fertilizer. It's strange to me that garden centres sell known invasive species, many don't carry any native species, and carry a lot of plants from Asia or Europe.

a_revoir.message:
Lasclay: The Milkweed Company yes, many birds do eat the seeds, and others use the fluff for nesting material; from the u.s. fish and wildlife service website: "Warblers, wrens, thrushes, orioles, and vireos interact with milkweed throughout their lifecycles. American goldfinches use the downy fibers of milkweed seeds for nest-building, chickadees gather seed fluff for insulation, and sparrows and juncos feed on milkweed seeds in fall and winter."

that said, at least here in new england, there's more than enough fluff as well as the attached seeds, for any birds that want it, so i'm not too worried about starving birds or cold babies.  if you aren't sending the seeds into the waste stream, then that would be a plus.

a_revoir.message: Jenny Barbour The leaves and stems of our native milkweeds naturally die back to the ground in fall. a_revoir.message: Jenny Novak Zupancic Euell Gibbons’ classic book in the 1970s of wild edibles, Stalking Wild Asparagus, has a whole chapter on milkweed. It has its own taste but sorta similar in appearance to asparagus as shoots, broccoli as unopened flower buds and okra as small pods (<1 in long). The milky substance has oxalic acid, so bring to a boil and discard the water 3 times before straining and consuming. Add salt to taste. He also includes a recipe for milkweed flower wine. It’s a beautiful reddish purple color but I found it to be an “acquired taste.” A good-size patch of milkweed provides plenty for the monarchs and judicious foraging for edibles.

a_revoir.message:
Connie Hayes Crop growing for the livestock contained inside 24/7 is wiping out all natural habitats and the chemicals they use have crept into the whole food chain.
 When I got my rural place 12 years ago, when you sat outside on a summer day you could hear the bees humming away in the garden and wildflowers…..  And cows were grazing across the road and on the hillsides….The last two years - no sound of bees or cows munching…):  
   The farm truck traffic is loud with heavy equipment and liquid manure tankers that then spread all that back onto the fields for the next crops the cows eat.  All the dairy farms and cows grazing on the hillsides are gone …. They are all in this growing dairy industrial farm 2 miles down the road that now has 2,000 cows inside that never see land, much less graze and eat green grass.   
  I stopped drinking milk, once I saw the food cycle feeding them.  Milk is lousy to make cream sauce now.  But I missed it! So now I spend almost $7 for a half gallon of milk from a dairy farm like when I grew up, and make it last 2 weeks!  Delicious cream sauce that stays thick and creamy .  From cows on a normal diet. 
  AND I LET THE MILKWEED GROW WILD ON MY ACRE AMIDST MY PLANTED GARDENS!!!! 
 Sorry for the long comment.  Felt it needed to be said.  HABITAT
